title: Calories vs Kilocalories: The Food-Label Fudge
h1: Calories, kilocalories, kilojoules — the food-label ambiguity
description: A 'calorie' on a US food label is actually a kilocalorie. Here is why nutrition co-opted the unit and how to reconcile it with the joule.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

hero: The 'Calorie' with a capital C on your food label is 1,000 scientific calories. The dual meaning is a century-old shorthand that no one has fixed.
body: In physics, one calorie is the energy needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C — about 4.184 J. In nutrition, 'one calorie' means 1,000 of those, i.e. one kilocalorie. The food industry has never distinguished them clearly, and this is why every EU food label carries both kJ and kcal.

> 1 cal (thermochemical) = 4.184 J (exact by definition)
> 1 Cal (food, capitalised) = 1 kcal = 1,000 cal = 4,184 J = 4.184 kJ
> 1 kJ = 0.2390 kcal
> 2,000 Cal/day = 8,368 kJ/day
## Why nutrition uses the big calorie

Wilbur Atwater, the pioneer of food calorimetry in the 1890s, used the kilocalorie because human diets involve millions of small calories per day. Writing '2,000,000 cal' on a label is absurd. He proposed capitalising the C — 'Calorie' — to mark the 1000× version. Modern labelling dropped the capitalisation but kept the meaning.

Since 1990, EU regulation requires food energy be shown in both kJ (primary) and kcal (secondary). A 100 g portion of pasta might read '1,470 kJ / 350 kcal' — the same energy in two units. Multiply kcal by 4.184 to check.

500 kcal × 4.184 = 2,092 kJ. In older CGS units: 5 × 10⁵ small calories. In watt-hours: 500 × 1.163 = 582 Wh — enough to run a laptop for 8 hours. In hard physics units, human daily intake (~10 MJ) is roughly the energy of 2 kg of TNT.
Food Calorie = kcal = 4.184 kJ. Multiply kJ by 0.24 for kcal. And never confuse a scientific paper's 'cal' with a nutrition label's 'Cal'.

faqs.a: US FDA allows ±20% tolerance for declared calorie counts. Actual calories from mixed foods are often 5–10% higher due to Atwater factor rounding.
Australian nutrition regulations lead with kJ; kcal is secondary. A 8,700 kJ = 2,080 kcal daily target is common.

faqs.q: Are food calories the same as burned calories?
faqs.a: Approximately — Atwater assumes 4 kcal/g for carbs and protein, 9 kcal/g for fat, 7 kcal/g for alcohol. Actual absorbed energy varies with fibre and cooking.
